cards.explanation: The answer is the sheep of His pasture. Asaph, whose name is on this psalm, asks, “Why does Your anger smolder against the sheep of Your pasture?” (Psalm 74:1) Sheep are not exactly the toughest creatures on the farm. I think that makes the question hit even softer.
The answer is Zion, friends. Asaph says it plainly: “…Mount Zion, where You dwell.” (Psalm 74:2) Right there in his prayer, he names the mountain.

The answer is False, friends. Asaph asks God, “Turn Your steps to the everlasting ruins, to everything in the sanctuary the enemy has destroyed.” (Psalm 74:3) That's no couple of dents. He points God to everything the enemy destroyed there.

The answer is all the carvings, friends. The foes were “…smashing all the carvings with hatchets and picks.” (Psalm 74:6) All of them, not just the ones in the front. Tools like that are made for a job, and this was a sad one.

The answer is that they burned it to the ground. The text says, “They have burned Your sanctuary to the ground…” (Psalm 74:7) The psalm also tells of smashing the carvings with hatchets and picks. It's a heavy verse, and I think it's okay to just let it be heavy.

The answer is False, friends. The enemy did not leave the other places standing. Asaph says, “They burned down every place where God met us in the land.” (Psalm 74:8) That's every place, with none left standing. It's a heavy line.
The answer is any prophet, bakers. Asaph says, “There is no longer any prophet.” (Psalm 74:9) No signs and no prophet. I think that's a very quiet kind of loneliness.

The word is taunt, friends. “How long, O God, will the enemy taunt You?” (Psalm 74:10) A taunt is an insult aimed at someone, and here Asaph says it's aimed at God. He brings that question straight to Him.
The answer is True, bakers. Asaph asks, “Will the foe revile Your name forever?” (Psalm 74:10) The insults aren't just about the people. They're aimed at God's own name.

The answer is that Asaph asks God to stretch it out to destroy the enemy, friends. Asaph says, “Why do You withdraw Your strong right hand? Stretch it out to destroy them!” (Psalm 74:11) He's honest about what he wants. Nothing polite in that line, just a plain ask.

The answer is True, friends. Right after the hard questions, Asaph says, “Yet God is my King from ancient times, working salvation on the earth.” (Psalm 74:12) He asks the tough stuff and then names who God is. Both of those live in the same prayer.

The creature is Leviathan, bakers. Asaph says to God, “You crushed the heads of Leviathan…” (Psalm 74:14) Then he says, “You fed him to the creatures of the desert.” (Psalm 74:14) That's the creature he names.

The answer is True, friends. Asaph says to God, “You dried up the ever-flowing rivers.” (Psalm 74:15) These are rivers that were ever-flowing, and the verse says He dried them up. That's a lot of water to deal with.
The word is winter, friends. Asaph says, “You made the summer and winter.” (Psalm 74:17) Both ends of the year are His. That's a lot of oven weather and a lot of cold mornings covered.

The word is spurned, bakers. Asaph says, “…a foolish people has spurned Your name.” (Psalm 74:18) To spurn is to turn something away with scorn. He's telling God exactly what's being done to His name.

The answer is His afflicted, friends. Asaph prays, “do not forget the lives of Your afflicted forever.” (Psalm 74:19) He's asking for the hurting ones by name. I think that's a prayer with a lot of love in it.
The answer is His covenant, bakers. Asaph says, “Consider Your covenant…” (Psalm 74:20) A covenant is a binding promise, and he brings it right into his prayer. He's asking God to consider it.

The reason is that violence fills the dark places of the land, friends. “Consider Your covenant, for haunts of violence fill the dark places of the land.” (Psalm 74:20) Asaph gives the reason right in the line. It's a heavy one, so I think it's fair to say that out loud.
The word is praise, bakers. Asaph prays, “may the poor and needy praise Your name.” (Psalm 74:21) That's what he asks for the poor and needy. I think that's a good prayer for anyone.

The answer is False, bakers. Asaph says, “Rise up, O God; defend Your cause!” (Psalm 74:22) He calls it God's cause, not Israel's alone. Then he adds, “Remember how the fool mocks You all day long.” (Psalm 74:22)

The answer is the uproar of His enemies, friends. In the last line, Asaph prays, “Do not disregard the clamor of Your adversaries, the uproar of Your enemies that ascends continually.” (Psalm 74:23) The noise doesn't stop, and he's laying it all before God.
